britannica-1911-arsuf:
Arsuf is a town on the shore of Palestine, north of Jaffa. It is famed as the place where the men of the cross beat the host of Saladin. King Richard of England led that host south from Acre in the year eleven ninety-one. His goal was Jaffa, and then the holy city.

The entry dwells on the march more than the fight. The host moved by the sea in a tight block, with gear by the shore and horse in the core. Horse bowmen stung the line for days, yet it held firm. At Arsuf the foe burst from the hills, and the rear bore the brunt.
britannica-1911-brondsted-peter-oluf:
Peter Oluf Brondsted (1780–1842) was a Danish archaeologist and traveller born at Fruering in Jutland on 17 November 1780. After study at the University of Copenhagen he visited Paris in 1806 with his friend Georg Koes, stayed two years, then went with him to Italy. Both men were zealously set on the study of antiquities, and shared tastes shaped their travels.

In 1810 they joined an expedition to Greece, where they dug out the temples of Zeus in Aegina and of Apollo at Bassae in Arcadia. After three years of active research Brondsted returned to Copenhagen and was made professor of Greek at the university. Finding Copenhagen short of facilities for publishing his vast travel materials. He exchanged the chair in 1818 for the post of Danish envoy at the papal court and settled in Rome.
britannica-1911-rutebeuf:
Rutebeuf (flourished 1245-1285) was a French trouvère poet of humble birth. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes his name appears in no record by peers. He plays on the name in verse as rude ox or rude work. Paris was his home by schooling and by life, it says.

His own poems tell of a hard marriage and deep money woes. Love of dice games drove much of that want, by his account. Patrons still paid him for saints lives and noble elegies in verse. As satirist he lashed friars and backed Paris scholars in their fights. Calls to crusade fill a run of his poems from the twelve sixties.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-brebe:
Jean de Brébeuf, a Jesuit missionary born in Normandy in 1593 and dead in Canada in 1649, gave his life to the Huron mission. Hoping at first to be a lay brother, he entered the Society as a scholastic in 1617, though illness at twenty-eight cut his studies short.

Landing at Quebec in 1625, Brébeuf lived five winter months in Indigenous wigwams and wrote a vivid account of it. He then canoed to Lake Huron and founded the first mission near Georgian Bay at Ihonatiria, labouring alone after his companion was recalled. Recalled to Quebec in 1628 as the colony faced ruin, he returned to the Hurons and died among them.
doe-osti-2575657-fused-deposition-modeli:
Final technical report DE-FE0032143, from Ohio University, authored by Logan Veley, Grace Baranack, Chinonso Ugwumadu, and colleagues under Yahya Al-Majali. Covering April 2022 to April 2025, it turns coal into 3D printing feedstock. Filaments loaded with up to seventy percent coal by weight were extruded and run on ordinary commercial printers. The printed composites were then carbonized, and the team measured their mechanical, thermal, and microstructural behavior.

Modeling worked at several scales, from atomistic interactions up to the voids and seams that printing leaves behind, to explain how defects govern strength. Large-scale trials printed real parts: molds for wind turbine blades and modular wall sections for construction. Cost analyses found the coal composites cost-effective and scalable for such tooling. The project gives a low-value, abundant material a route into manufacturing, where printed tooling is normally cut from far pricier stock.
doe-osti-3413711-measured-baseline-of-a-:
Dated June 2026, report ORNL/SPR-2026/4700 from Oak Ridge National Laboratory sets a measured baseline for a double-wide manufactured home testbed. Hevar Palani leads a seven-author team. The study tracks both energy use and moisture behavior, called hygrothermal performance in the text.

Surface readings gave solar reflectance of 0.74 for vinyl siding and 0.10 for roof shingles. Crawlspace skirts averaged 0.92, a bright, heat-shedding value. Tables give heat resistance for each material layer at 75 degrees Fahrenheit. A firm measured baseline lets later retrofits prove real gains in comfort and power bills for families. Moisture and heat readings together form the measured baseline for this testbed home.
